Nineteenth Indian Expedition to Antarctica, Scientific Report, 2004 
Department of Ocean Development, Technical Publication No. 17, pp. 89-97 
The Geospace Event on the Night of 11 August 2000:
Results of Ground Geomagnetic Field Measurements
From Maitri, Antarctica
K. Jeeva
1
, S. Gurubaran
1
, A. Dhar
2
 and G. Rajaram
2
1
 Equatorial Geophysical Research Laboratory, Indian Institute of Geomagnetism,
Tirunelveli-627 011
2
 Indian Institute of Geomagnetism, Mumbai- 400 005
Abstract
Intense bursts of magnetic field variations were recorded on the night of 11 August
2000 by the fluxgate magnetometer installed at the Indian Antarctic Station Maitri (70.8"S,
11.8°E). These variations are ascribed to the southward turnings of the interplanetary
magnetic field (IMF) and enhancements in solar wind particle pressure. With an L-value
of 4.8, these records track the geospace processes occurring on the night sector of the
magnetosphere-ionosphere system.
Introduction
The geographical location of Maitri is unique in that under quiet
conditions the station is under the influence of the mid-latitude Sq current
system. As the magn etic disturbances grow due to the enhanced solar
wind-magnetosphere interaction, Maitri comes increasingly under the
auroral oval. The auroral oval expands under such conditions to envelop
the sky over Maitri.
Past experiments conducted at the Indian Antarctic Station clearly
distinguished the disturbed time behaviour of the geomagnetic field
variation from their quiet-time characteristics (Kalra et at, 1995). Many
important processes occur on the night side of the Earth wherein the
geomagnetic field is stretched to form a long 'tail' by the streaming charged
particle flow from the Sun. The field lines forming the tail are 'energized'
wherever the interplanetary magnetic field turns southward as this favours
magnetic field reconnection on the dayside of the Earth. The reconnected
field is swept across towards the night side. The magnetic field ultimately
releases the energy in the form of sporadic bursts in the tail region that
manifest as substorms in the ground geomagnetic data. The channel in
90 K. Jeeva, et al. 
which this energy is routed through is the substorm current wedge that
takes a westward path in the high latitude ionosphere. Field-aligned currents
constitute the edges of this current pattern (Kisabeth and Rosotoker, 1974).
Controversies still persist as to whether this loading-unloading process
is solely responsible for the substorm phenomenon or the directly driven
process plays an equally important role in causing the substorm signatures
(Rostoker,1987). The storm-substorm relationship is another area that is
gathering increasing attention in recent times.
In this report we have made qualitative assessment of how the
geomagnetic field variations as measured on the ground r espond to the
changing solar wind conditions. Though the results are not new, they
provide justification for continuing such studies.
Selection of Data
A fluxgate magnetometer is operated by the Indian Institute of
Geomagnetism round the year at Maitri. The magn etometer records daily
variations in the X, Y and Z vector components of the geomagnetic field,
as well as the pulsations in the same. The data are recorded in both analog
(on chart-recorders) and digital (on solid state data loggers) form. Further,,
the absorption level of the radio noise at 30 MHz as recorded by the riometer
is also monitored continuously. A decrease in the r adio intensity at this
frequency or an increase in the absorption level would correspond to an
increase in the D-region ionization density caused by th e precipitation of
charged particles along the geomagnetic field lines. These changes would
correspond to a field-aligned current that can be detected in the Y-
component of the magnetic field.
During the year 2000, the solar activity has reached its peak and many
intense solar geophysical events took place then. In this report we focus
upon the geomagnetic conditions that prevailed on the night of 11 August
